newsitem.title: USA: Fed's Kelley says banks must cut settlement risk.
newsitem.headline: Fed's Kelley says banks must cut settlement risk.

text.p: Banks must step up their efforts to reduce the legal and other risks involved in international settlements, Federal Reserve Governor Edward Kelley said Thursday.

In a speech prepared for delivery to a New York conference on electronic payments systems, Kelley said more than $1 trillion a day now is turned over in foreign exchange markets and $2 trillion a day flows through Fedwire and the Clearing House Interbank Payment System called CHIPS.
A text of his remarks was issued in Washington.
"Risks have escalated in international settlements and these are motivating both commercial and central banks to take action," Kelley said.
"Given the enormous flow of funds involved, aggregate exposure for major dealing banks can be very large in proportion to capital," he added.

Kelley said the Federal Reserve's decision to open its Fedwire for longer hours starting next year -- 18 hours a day instead of 10 -- was one response to the need to make clearing and settlement arrangements more efficent.
The expanded Fedwire hours would cover the entire European banking day and about 2-1/2 hours of the Tokyo banking day.

"Staff believes that overlaps in operating hours among major financial centers would strengthen interbank settlement for cross-border markets," said the Fed's proposal that was passed by the Fed board Wednesday.

"It is thought that the long-run benefits from offering final payment capabilities will strengthen interbank settlements and contribute to reductions in foreign exchange settlement risk through innovations in payment and settlement practices," the proposal said.
Kelley said it remained to be seen whether established clearing organizations will take advantage of the earlier Fedwire hours and consider speeding up their money settlement process.
In addition, there is a question whether early-morning money market trading will emerge, including especially federal funds trading. Kelley said.
